items.english: "That, I take it, is a kind of conclusion, eh." This was Nekohachi trying to take back what he felt he had fumbled a little earlier over the ending of the Tiger. "But then, when I get called to the princes and the like, why, gyagya-gya," and with that baring his teeth, goggling his eyes, screwing his face into something queer, he showed them cats at it fighting, and set them all off at once. But keeping a straight face himself, he went on, "It is not barnyard fowl, showing you cats kicking at each other is still hardly out of place. When the person before me is a lady, I can well hear the laugh from behind the fan where she hides her noble face. But at times, when I went up to Mr ___ for instance, I was told, they say you are good not only at mimicry but at rakugo too, let our guests hear something funny, so I declined. It is far too awesome for me, I cannot. But I was pressed, so perform a turn I did, perform one I did, and it is a strange thing, from the very start not a bit of it gets across. As we only know our own low-down society, of course the story falls there too. 'Oi, Hachi, are you there,' says I," and with that he showed hitching his backside and sitting on the step at the entrance, "from the first that does not get across what it is about, 'beranmei, bare-arsed you cannot hitch up, eh,' none of that ready wit gets across. Begging pardon for a rude thing to say, there is nothing to bite on, where there ought to come a roar they all sit prim."
notes: I kept the blanks as Mr ___: the source writes OOO-sama, discretion performed in the telling, so I did not fill it.
Hachi is left as Hachi: the rakugo stock butt the bible flags at p155, quoted inside Nekohachi's failed upstairs turn.
gyagya-gya and the beranmei hitch-up line are kept as act, not smoothed into description: the joke about a bare backside that cannot hitch itself up is meant to fall flat upstairs.
